t09176:
💡 Understanding
For someone with cognitive decline, the repeated phrase "I want to go home" is observed as a mix of memory, orientation and a need for security. They may mistake their childhood home for their current one.
t09177:
🎯 5-step approach
① Empathize first: "You want to go home" — don't deny it
② Redirect attention: shift the topic with favorite food, photos or music
③ Unpack together: slowly, one item at a time, naturally
④ Check for sundowning: if frequent at 4–7pm, brighten the lighting
⑤ If wandering risk: ID tag + location tracker are essential
t09178: ⚠️ Caution: If they start packing at night it can lead to wandering, so a companion is essential.
t09179:
💡 Understanding
Angry outbursts come from loss of impulse control due to reduced frontal-lobe function + frustration from communication difficulty + physical discomfort (pain, difficulty urinating). They may struggle to control it themselves.
t09180:
🎯 5-step approach
① Don't confront: never argue or try to persuade
② Safe distance: stay 1.5m+ away and lower your posture
③ Calm voice: "Are you feeling upset?" slowly
④ Check physical causes: constipation, back pain, toothache, hunger
⑤ Check the environment: remove loud TV or unfamiliar people
t09181: ⚠️ Caution: If it recurs often, seek counseling from a professional service. The caregiver's safety comes first.
t09182:
💡 Understanding
Due to long-term memory damage, they travel back in time. They may see a wife as their mother, or a child as a sibling. It is not a lack of love but damage to the brain's neural network.
t09183:
🎯 5-step approach
① Use names often: "Dad, it's me, your youngest, Youngsu"
② Prompt reminiscence: look at old photos, wedding or travel pictures together
③ Consistent titles: introduce yourself the same way each time
④ Steady your heart: caregiver, don't be hurt — it's not their fault
⑤ Welcome repetition: greet warmly each day as if meeting for the first time
t09184: 💡 Hope: Even when they can't recognize you, the emotional bond (a warm touch) remains until the very end.
t09185:
💡 Understanding
The sleep-wake cycle changes seen with cognitive decline are caused by hypothalamic damage. Reduced ability to tell day from night + lower melatonin + sundowning overlap.
t09186:
🎯 6-step approach
① Naps under 30 min: only between 1–3pm
② 30 min of sunlight: a morning walk to reset the body clock
③ Block evening stimulation: no caffeine, news or intense TV
④ Evening ritual: warm milk, gentle music, dim light
⑤ Bedroom setup: 22℃ · dark and quiet
⑥ Over 2 weeks: consider seeing a neurologist
t09187: ⚠️ Caution: Never self-medicate with sleeping pills. Risk of falls and delirium.
t09188:
💡 Understanding
Reported when cognitive decline has progressed considerably. Visual hallucinations (seeing a deceased person) come from occipital-lobe damage, auditory ones from temporal-lobe damage. To them it is entirely real.
t09189:
🎯 5-step approach
① Don't deny: never say "there's no such thing"
② Empathize: "That must have been scary. I'm here with you"
③ Tidy the environment: shadows, mirrors and busy patterns → trigger hallucinations
④ Brighten lighting: hallucinations ↑ in dark places
⑤ Medication: if frequent, consider seeing a neurologist
t09190: ⚠️ Caution: If hallucinations lead to self-harm or harm to others, go to the ER immediately.
t09191:
💡 Understanding
90% of wandering has intent — "I have to get to work," "I have to see my mother." It results from lost time-orientation + long-term memory intruding on the present. A need to move the legs also plays a part.
t09192:
🎯 5-step approach
① Physical barriers: double-lock the front door + move the shoes
② ID tag essential: contact info on clothes, bag, watch
③ Location tracker: GPS watch (coming soon) · phone
④ Meet the need: "Let's take a walk together" — go out with them
⑤ Pre-register: fingerprint registration with the police Safe-Dream service (essential)
t09193: 🚨 If missing: report to 112 + local station + Safe-Dream at once. The first hour is the golden time.
t09194:
💡 Understanding
Reported when cognitive decline has progressed considerably. Reduced smell and taste + swallowing difficulty (dysphagia) + depression + denture discomfort + a "someone poisoned it" delusion act together.
t09195:
🎯 5-step approach
① Check the mouth: dentures, toothache, mouth sores
② Adjust texture: soft and finely cut (rice cake and nuts are risky)
③ Small and frequent: spread over 5–6 times
④ Favorite foods: prioritize dishes they used to enjoy
⑤ Eat together: share the meal with the caregiver for a good mood
t09196: ⚠️ Caution: If intake stays under 50% for over a week → malnutrition risk; seek care immediately.
t09197:
💡 Understanding
Caused by forgetting where the toilet is + reduced ability to sense the urge + forgetting the order of undressing. They feel embarrassed too. Never get angry.
t09198:
🎯 5-step approach
① Mark the toilet: big pictures and arrows
② Guide every 2 hours: "Let's pop to the toilet"
③ Simplify clothing: no buttons · elastic-waist trousers
④ Night pads: less shame + cleanliness
⑤ Preserve dignity: never criticize · clean up calmly
t09199: 💡 Tip: If there is a sudden change, consult a medical institution.
t09200:
💡 Understanding
Commonly seen with short-term memory changes. Even after just hearing the answer, it doesn't stay, so they ask again. This is the part caregivers find most exhausting.
t09201:
🎯 5-step approach
① As if for the first time: answer "What's for lunch today?" like you're hearing it fresh
② Short and clear: simple answers (no long explanations)
③ Note board: put frequent answers on the wall in large letters
④ Redirect attention: change the topic with music, a walk or a snack
⑤ Caregiver rest: take turns with family · use a day-care center
t09202: 💡 Tip: If the caregiver burns out, call the Dementia Care Center (1666-0921) for counseling.
t09203:
💡 Understanding
Delusions like "someone stole my wallet" or "my husband is cheating" are the brain's way of compensating for memory damage. They forget where they put something and conclude someone took it.
t09204:
🎯 5-step approach
① No arguing: never deny with "no one stole it"
② Search together: "Let's look for it together"
③ Keep spares: a spare wallet or glasses (pretend to find it)
④ Fixed spot: keep important items always in the same place
⑤ If severe: consider seeing a neurologist
t09205: ⚠️ Caution: If it leads to verbal or physical abuse, ask a professional service for help immediately.
t09206:
💡 Understanding
When there are memory changes, the mood can sink too. Awareness of one's own decline + hopelessness + social isolation + reduced serotonin are the causes.
t09207:
🎯 5-step approach
① Build a routine: walk and eat at the same time each day
② Small wins: folding laundry, watering a plant, etc.
③ Social connection: day-care center · visits from friends
④ Reminiscence therapy: positive feelings through old photos and music
⑤ Professional counseling: if it lasts over 2 weeks, consult a professional service
t09208: 🚨 Emergency: mention of suicide or self-harm → psychiatry immediately.
t09209:
💡 Understanding
As cognitive function declines, fall risk can rise. Reduced spatial cognition + loss of muscle strength + medication side effects (dizziness) + narrowed field of vision are combined causes.
t09210:

① Safe environment: remove rugs · clear the floor · corner guards
② Bathroom grab bars: essential beside the toilet and bathtub
③ Stronger lighting: night lights · bright hallways
④ Safe footwear: non-slip · no laces
⑤ Exercise: light balance exercises (chair gymnastics)
⑥ Review medication: if they take any medication, consult their care team

t09346:
🔬 Reference basis
The omega-3 fatty acids (EPA·DHA) abundant in mackerel, salmon and sardines are core components of neuronal cell membranes, reducing brain inflammation and strengthening synaptic signaling. An Annals of Neurology 2019 study reported a 23% lower Alzheimer's risk with intake 2+ times per week.
t09347:
🎯 Recommended intake
① 2–3 times/week, ~100g per serving (palm-sized)
② Cooking: grill, steam, or soup (no frying — destroys omega-3)
③ Suggested: mackerel, salmon, sardine, saury
④ Tip: pair with perilla or olive oil
t09348: ⚠️ Caution: If you have health concerns or take medication, consult a health professional. Limit large fish with mercury concerns (canned tuna) to once a week or less.
t09349:
🔬 Reference basis
Leafy greens like spinach, kale and chard are rich in vitamin K, folate and lutein, slowing cognitive aging. A Neurology 2018 study found one serving daily kept cognitive aging 11 years younger. Folate is known to relate to homocysteine levels.
t09350:
🎯 Recommended intake
① 1–2 servings daily (1 cup raw)
② Cooking: lightly blanch, raw salad, or seasoned
③ Suggested: spinach, kale, perilla leaf, chard, mallow
④ Tip: fat-soluble vitamins — eat with some oil
t09351: ⚠️ Caution: If taking warfarin (a blood thinner), vitamin K can interfere with the medication — keep intake consistent.
t09352:
🔬 Reference basis
The anthocyanins in blueberries, strawberries and raspberries are powerful antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress on brain cells. A Harvard Annals of Neurology 2012 study found women who ate berries frequently had cognitive aging delayed by 2.5 years.
t09353:
🎯 Recommended intake
① 3–5 times/week, 1/2 cup per serving (~80g)
② Ways: fresh, with yogurt, or in a smoothie
③ Suggested: blueberry, strawberry, raspberry, blackberry
④ Tip: frozen berries have the same nutrients — available year-round
t09354: ⚠️ Caution: If limiting sugar, cut to 1/4 cup per serving and favor low-GI blueberries.
t09355:
🔬 Reference basis
The vitamin E abundant in walnuts, almonds and cashews prevents neuronal membrane oxidation, and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) improves brain blood flow. A JAMA 2014 study reported a daily handful (28g) was associated with a 27% reduction in cognitive decline.
t09356:
🎯 Recommended intake
① A handful daily (~28g, 7–10 nuts)
② Form: raw or lightly roasted (no salt/sugar)
③ Suggested: walnut · almond · cashew · hazelnut
④ Tip: top morning cereal or yogurt
t09357: ⚠️ Caution: Nuts are calorie-dense — overeating causes weight gain. With gout, cut back on cashews and peanuts. Watch for allergies.
t09358:
🔬 Reference basis
Green tea's EGCG (epigallocatechin gallate) has strong antioxidant/anti-inflammatory action that inhibits beta-amyloid aggregation. A Japanese American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2006 study found a 54% lower cognitive-impairment risk in people 70+ drinking 2+ cups daily.
t09359:
🎯 Recommended intake
① 2–3 cups daily (~200ml each)
② Brewing: steep in 80℃ water 2–3 min (not boiling — destroys catechins)
③ Suggested: ujeon, sejak, matcha (matcha = whole leaf)
④ Tip: drink 1 hour after meals to lower caffeine absorption
t09360: ⚠️ Caution: If caffeine-sensitive, drink before 2 PM. If taking supplements, don't drink with meals (blocks absorption).
t09361:
🔬 Reference basis
The Mediterranean diet (olive oil + fish + vegetables + nuts) is the known standard for brain-health eating. A 5-year New England Journal of Medicine 2013 PREDIMED study showed a 35% reduction related to cognitive maintenance. The MIND diet (a Mediterranean variant) showed a 53% Alzheimer's reduction.
t09362:
🎯 Recommended intake
① 5+ days/week Mediterranean pattern
② Oil: extra-virgin olive oil (raw over heated)
③ Suggested: olive oil, avocado, whole grains, legumes
④ Tip: combines fine with Korean food (multigrain rice + fish + greens + olive oil)
t09363: ⚠️ Caution: Olive oil is calorie-dense too — keep to 1–2 tbsp/day. Avoid processed foods, red meat, and refined sugar.
t09364:
🔬 Reference basis
Moderate aerobic exercise raises BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), growing the hippocampus (memory center). A University of Pittsburgh PNAS 2011 study found walking 3×/week for a year gave a 2% hippocampal volume increase — equal to reversing 2 years of cognitive aging.
t09365:
🎯 Recommended exercise
① 5×/week · 30–40 min
② Intensity: slightly breathless (can still chat)
③ Timing: 30 min of morning/afternoon sun (vitamin D + serotonin)
④ Tip: walk with family or pets (more social stimulation)
t09366: ⚠️ Caution: With knee/hip discomfort, stick to flat ground. If concerned about your health, consult a professional before starting. In heat waves or cold snaps, walk indoors.
t09367:
🔬 Reference basis
Strength training raises both IGF-1 and BDNF, boosting brain plasticity. An Archives of Internal Medicine 2010 study proved improved cognitive scores when older adults did strength training 2×/week for a year. It also prevents sarcopenia (muscle loss), lowering fall risk.
t09368:
🎯 Recommended exercise
① 2–3×/week · 20–30 min
② Method: chair sit-to-stand, 10 reps × 3 sets
③ Tools: 1–2kg dumbbells, water bottles, resistance bands
④ Tip: start with large muscles (legs → back → chest → arms)
t09369: ⚠️ Caution: If concerned about your health, don't hold your breath. No heavy weights (low intensity, high reps). Stop immediately if it hurts.
t09370:
🔬 Reference basis
Balance declines ~1% per year after age 70. Balance exercise stimulates the cerebellum and vestibular system, cutting fall risk. A Cochrane Review 2019 meta-analysis confirmed a 22% fall reduction after 12 weeks of balance training.
t09371:
🎯 Recommended exercise
① 5–10 min daily
② One-leg stand: hold a chair, 10 sec × 3
③ Toe walk & heel walk: 10 steps each
④ Tip: do a one-leg stand while brushing teeth or cooking
t09372: ⚠️ Caution: Always in a safe spot (beside a chair/wall). With dizziness or tinnitus, see a doctor. A caregiver present is recommended.
t09373:
🔬 Reference basis
Dance is a top dual-task activity, engaging movement + cognition + social interaction at once. A New England Journal of Medicine 2003 study found regular dancing was associated with a 76% reduction (double that of other exercise) in cognitive decline. Remembering choreography stimulates the hippocampus.
t09374:
🎯 Recommended exercise
① 2–3×/week · 30 min
② Suggested: trot, waltz, line dance, cha-cha
③ Method: light steps in time with music
④ Tip: use dance classes at community/senior centers
t09375: ⚠️ Caution: With knee pain or weak bones, do seated dance. Rest immediately if dizzy.
t09376:
🔬 Reference basis
Gardening is all-around exercise — light aerobic + strength + sensory stimulation — and soil microbes stimulate serotonin. A The Lancet 2006 study reported a 36% reduction related to cognitive maintenance. Nature exposure also helps reduce depression.
t09377:
🎯 Recommended activity
① 3–5×/week · 20–40 min
② Tasks: watering, weeding, moving pots
③ Alternatives: balcony pots, indoor plants, a small plot
④ Tip: choose color/scent plants (lavender, rosemary)
t09378: ⚠️ Caution: Avoid peak sun (12–3 PM); wear a hat and sunscreen. If your airways are sensitive, wear a mask.
